mission: Find four landmarks in and around the Loop. At each one, check in to earn its badge, unlock its story, and collect a Time Card. Do them in any order. Everything stays on this phone.
afterDone: All four badges earned. The rest of Chicago is waiting.
safetyNote: • Chicago weather swings fast and the lakefront wind is real. Dress for it, cross at crosswalks, and keep an eye on traffic and bikes near the park paths.

stops.name: Cloud Gate
stops.teaser: A giant mirror bean. Everyone calls it something else.
stops.map: Cloud Gate, 201 E Randolph St, Chicago, IL
stops.clue: Head to AT&T Plaza in Millennium Park. Look for a huge polished steel sculpture shaped like a kidney bean, and walk into the arch underneath.
stops.safety: Millennium Park is crowded on summer weekends. Watch your step on the plaza, keep young kids close, and stay on the ground. The sculpture is for looking, not climbing.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

q.prompt: Step into the arch underneath the sculpture and look up at your reflection. What does it do?
options: It splits into many warped copies
q.hint: Look straight up, not at the outside.
q.verify: The arch underneath is called the omphalos. Its curved mirror multiplies and bends reflections (Wikipedia, Cloud Gate). Check on site. Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

then.label: Under construction
then.line: Cloud Gate under construction in 2004, with a crane and a large steel ring on the site.

link.t: Look for historic photos at the Library of Congress

now.head: Today
now.label: From under Cloud Gate
now.line: The Chicago skyline seen from underneath the sculpture. Photo from 2013.

story: Artist Anish Kapoor designed it, and it was built from 2004 to 2006. It was partly unveiled at the Millennium Park opening on July 15, 2004, finished in August 2005, and formally dedicated on May 15, 2006.
It is made of 168 stainless steel plates, joined and polished so the seams are hard to find. It is about 33 feet tall, 66 feet long and 42 feet wide, and weighs about 110 short tons.

The public nicknamed it "The Bean" while it was under construction. Kapoor did not like the nickname at first but later accepted it. The arch underneath has its own name, the omphalos, Greek for navel.
stops.fact: Kapoor's official title is Cloud Gate. The Bean was the crowd's idea.
stops.disputed: Nothing big is disputed here. The thing people most often get wrong is who came up with the name.

claims.t: Cloud Gate is made of 168 stainless steel plates.
claims.why: Wikipedia gives 168 plates, polished so the seams are hard to see.

claims.t: Artist Anish Kapoor named the sculpture "The Bean."
claims.why: The public came up with the nickname during construction. Kapoor's title is Cloud Gate.

stops.name: Chicago Water Tower
stops.teaser: A tiny castle that outlasted a city on fire.
stops.map: Chicago Water Tower, 806 N Michigan Ave, Chicago, IL
stops.clue: Walk the Magnificent Mile on North Michigan Avenue. Find a small pale stone castle with turrets, wedged between skyscrapers.
stops.safety: North Michigan Avenue sidewalks are packed and the corner is a busy intersection. Cross only at the signal and keep out of the street while taking photos.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

q.prompt: Look at the tower's walls. What color is the stone?
q.verify: Sources say it is built of yellow Joliet limestone (Chicago Architecture Center). Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

then.label: Just finished
then.line: The tower was completed in 1869 as a standpipe for the city's water system.

link.t: Look for historic photos at the Library of Congress

now.head: Today
now.label: The tower today
now.line: The little limestone castle among the skyscrapers on Michigan Avenue. Photo from 2004.

story: The Water Tower was completed in 1869. William W. Boyington designed it in a castle-like Gothic Revival style, in yellow Joliet limestone.
It is not a real castle. The tower hid a standpipe, a tall pipe added to smooth out pressure surges from the city's pumps. The fancy outside covers a simple job.

In October 1871 the Great Chicago Fire burned much of the city, but the Water Tower and its pumping station were not badly damaged. They were built with little or no wood. They were not the only structures left standing.
stops.fact: The pretty castle is actually a disguise for a plumbing pipe.
stops.disputed: A guide's story credits a fireman, Frank Trautman, with saving it by covering it in wet blankets and canvas. That is one docent's account. The documented reason is that the tower was built of stone with almost no wood.

claims.t: The Chicago Water Tower was built in 1869, before the Great Fire.
claims.why: The Chicago Architecture Center gives 1869 as its completion date.

claims.t: The Water Tower was the only building left standing after the 1871 fire.
claims.why: The Chicago Architecture Center says it was not the only structure left standing.

sources.t: Chicago Architecture Center: Chicago Water Tower

stops.name: Buckingham Fountain
stops.teaser: A wedding cake for a lake.
stops.map: Buckingham Fountain, 301 S Columbus Dr, Chicago, IL
stops.clue: Cross into Grant Park and find a giant, many-layered fountain with stone sea horses around it.
stops.safety: The fountain runs only in warm months, usually early May to mid October. Stay off the basin walls and keep clear of the spray, which can soak the pavement.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

q.prompt: Walk around the fountain and count the sea horse statues. How many are there?
q.verify: Four pairs of sea horses stand for four states (Wikipedia, Buckingham Fountain). Count on site. Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

then.label: A 1939 poster
then.line: A Federal Art Project poster advertising the fountain as free, in 1939.

link.t: Look for historic photos at the Library of Congress

now.head: Today
now.label: The fountain today
now.line: Buckingham Fountain in front of the Chicago skyline. Photo from 2012.

story: The fountain was dedicated on August 26, 1927. Kate Sturges Buckingham gave it to the city in memory of her brother Clarence Buckingham.
Edward H. Bennett designed it, and French sculptor Marcel Loyau made the statues. It was inspired by the Latona Fountain at the Palace of Versailles.
The four pairs of sea horses stand for the four states that touch Lake Michigan: Illinois, Wisconsin, Michigan and Indiana. The whole fountain stands for the lake. The center jet can reach 150 feet.
stops.fact: The fountain holds about 1.5 million gallons and has 193 jets.
stops.disputed: Wikipedia calls it "one of the largest fountains in the world." Whether it is the largest depends on how you measure, so treat that as a claim, not a record.

claims.t: The sea horses at Buckingham Fountain stand for the four states that touch Lake Michigan.
claims.why: Wikipedia: four pairs of sea horses for Illinois, Wisconsin, Michigan and Indiana.

claims.t: Buckingham Fountain is the largest fountain in the world.
claims.why: Wikipedia says "one of the largest." Rankings depend on what is measured.

stops.name: Chicago Theatre
stops.teaser: A French palace on State Street, with the sign everyone knows.
stops.map: Chicago Theatre, 175 N State St, Chicago, IL
stops.clue: Walk to State Street in the Loop. Look for a tall vertical sign that spells the city's name above a grand arch.
stops.safety: State Street is busy with buses, bikes and pedestrians. Stay on the sidewalk and cross only at the lights.
stops.field: Field notes pending: nobody has walked this stop for the app yet.

q.prompt: Count the letters on the tall vertical sign. How many?
q.hint: It spells the name of the city.
q.verify: The vertical sign spells CHICAGO, which is 7 letters (Wikipedia, Chicago Theatre). Check that no extra words are on it. Written from sources, not yet checked on site.

then.label: Opening year
then.line: The Chicago Theatre opened in 1921 and was promoted as the "Wonder Theatre of the World."

link.t: Look for historic photos at the Library of Congress

now.head: Today
now.label: The sign at night
now.line: The vertical CHICAGO sign and marquee glowing on State Street. Photo from 2010.

story: The theatre opened on October 26, 1921. Brothers Cornelius and George Rapp (Rapp and Rapp) designed it, with a French Baroque interior. It was promoted as the "Wonder Theatre of the World."
It opened with 3,880 seats. A restoration in 1986 left about 3,600.

The marquee has been replaced several times, most recently in 1994, and keeps its earlier look. The original marquee went to the Smithsonian Institution in 2004. The theatre is a Chicago Landmark (1983) and is on the National Register of Historic Places (1979).
stops.fact: The Y-shaped symbol on the sign stands for the forked Chicago River.
stops.disputed: Nothing big is disputed here. The main trap is assuming the sign you see is the 1921 one.

claims.t: The marquee on the building today is the original one from 1921.
claims.why: It has been replaced several times, the whole marquee in 1994. The original went to the Smithsonian in 2004.
